splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year. The timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay, affecting billions of dollars in potential obligations across thousands of employers.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected before or by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, giving plans flexibility to use more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock does not run during the period of absconding, allowing revocation proceedings even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release terms, so the term continues to run even when the supervisee absconds, and the court loses revocation authority when the term expires.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any claim they previously presented, on top of § 2255(h)'s separate requirements. This affects thousands of federal prisoners seeking post-conviction relief.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a stricter gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without facing the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether and when candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects whether candidates can challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place, or whether such disputes must wait until after the election.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election procedures before an election absent a showing of concrete, particularized injury beyond generalized competitive harm.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Second Circuit's approach to legal standards for discrimination liability and damages in hospitality and business establishments was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant Supreme Court review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide by establishing or refining standards for fair treatment and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that other circuits may not follow.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims and available remedies in public accommodation and hospitality contexts.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has heightened significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines enhancements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Sentencing Guidelines Application Note 1, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, is entitled to deference under Stinson v. United States, especially after Kisor v. Wilkie narrowed the scope of deference to agency interpretations of their own rules. The split affects whether conspiracy convictions can trigger the career-offender enhancement.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) entitled to controlling weight under Stinson, and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the plain text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, so Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline and is not entitled to deference, particularly after Kisor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums for certain drug offenses, with significant liberty implications.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit held that such changes can never contribute, while the Seventh Circuit held that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement attempting to allow this exceeds its statutory authority. Other circuits have allowed such changes to be considered. The split affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences under outdated mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, particularly when combined with other factors, may constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and the Sentencing Commission's policy statement permitting this is valid.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing sentences upon revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust and the need for deterrence.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme end of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of the court's trust rather than punishment for the underlying violation conduct. This affects hundreds of individuals facing revocation proceedings each year.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should address breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sentences is to address the defendant's breach of the court's trust in granting supervised release, not to punish the defendant for the violation conduct itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines career-offender provision when the state statute covers substances not listed in the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be controlled under federal law. The Eighth Circuit holds that any state-controlled substance qualifies with no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the state offense to match federal drug schedules. The split creates sentencing disparities for defendants with state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state convictions qualify broadly
positions.summary: Holds that USSG § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal-law limitation applies — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, requiring a categorical match.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may instead bring civil rights claims under Bivens or other statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoner challenges that implicate the terms of confinement — such as BOP decisions on transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act — or whether such claims may also be brought as civil rights actions. The split affects how prisoners may challenge BOP administrative decisions regarding earned time credits, halfway house placement, and home confinement eligibility.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody based on First Step Act time credits, must be brought as habeas corpus petitions under § 2241.

positions.label: Civil rights claims are also available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may be brought through civil rights actions rather than exclusively through habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the applicable time limit to appeal a Hyde Amendment order for attorney's fees is the civil deadline (30 days) or the criminal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, noting a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a).

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is governed by the criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A). The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while the dissent argued this created a circuit split with other courts holding the appreciation belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of 'property of the estate.'

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's structure, policies, and legislative history designed to protect good-faith debtors who convert.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court's denial of a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, noting that delayed review risks irreparable harm. This approach may diverge from other circuits' treatment of similar sealing order appeals, where the collateral order doctrine is applied more narrowly.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal is not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the interest can be adequately vindicated by other means, such as post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
